5...h5?! was the start of the trouble. It was a loosening move and White's 6.c4 c5 7.d5 opened the centre while your king was still in the middle. 7...exd5 took a pawn but the evaluation was already -1.7.

8.Nh4 hit your pieces, and 8...Ng4 uncovered an attack from your queen on the h4 knight, a discovered attack. Then 9...g5 and 10.Bxd5 Bxd5 11.Qxd5 left your king's side wide open. By 12.Bxg5 Be7 13.Nf5 you were at -4.5.

review.focus: Your king was still in the centre at 13...Bxg5. 13...O-O was the engine move; get the king safe before you take material when the other side has checks.

sections.text: You played the Classical Italian with 4.c3 and 5.d4, the main line. After 5...exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Nxe4 the position was sharp and close to level. 8.O-O Bxc3 9.bxc3 d5 and 10.Re1 O-O followed, and the engine had you around -0.5.

12.Qc2?? was the blunder: the knight on c3 attacked both queen and bishop, and moving the queen sideways let 12...Nxb5 take the bishop. 12.Qb3 Nxb5 13.Qxb5 was the engine line, which kept you in the game.

sections.text: You played the Scotch Gambit with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4, and after 4...exd4 5.Nxd4 Black grabbed the e4 pawn with 5...Nxe4. The position was playable for White, but only if you found the right idea.
The right idea was 6.Nxc6, taking the knight on c6 before it could bother your knight on d4. Instead 6.Qf3? hit the knight on e4 but brought the queen out early, and 6...Nd6 pushed the bishop back.
7.Nb5?? was the blunder. 7.Nxc6 was available again and kept the game close, but the knight move left you at -3.6, and you resigned.
In short, you had two chances to take on c6, and each time you chose a different move.

review.turning_point: 6.Qf3? turned a normal opening into a worse position, and 7.Nb5?? made it worse; 7.Nxc6 would still have kept things close.
review.focus: When a gambit line leaves your knight on d4, check the capture on c6 first. At 6.Nxc6 and 7.Nxc6 you could have simplified the position.

review.headline: A Smith-Morra Gambit where 7.Bxe4 opened the d-file and left your king stuck in the middle

sections.text: You played the Smith-Morra with 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4, a common way to take the pawn back. The first moves were fine (+0.1 after 3.Qxd4) and the position was close to level. 5.Nd2 and 6.Bd3 followed, which the engine rated about equal.

The real problem was 7.Bxe4. After 6...dxe4 you could simply recapture with 7.Nxe4, which was the engine move. 7.Bxe4 allowed 7...Nxe4 8.Nxe4 and then 8...Qxd1+, since the knight had left the d-file. After 9.Kxd1 your king was stuck in the centre with no castling.

From there Black built up: 9...e5, 10...f5 and 11...e4 gave Black a strong centre, and the evaluation grew to -4.8 after 13.Ngxe4 fxe4 14.Nxe4. The moves 12.Ng5?! and 13.Ngxe4?! only made things worse.
Black's king went long with 15...O-O-O and 17...Bc2+ and 19...Bd3+ drove your king further. You resigned after 19 moves.

review.turning_point: 7.Bxe4 let the queens trade with check on d1 and lost the right to castle.
review.focus: At 7.Bxe4, recapture with the piece that keeps your structure: 7.Nxe4 was the engine move. Watch for open files with queens facing each other.

sections.text: This was a standard Petrov Modern Attack. You took the pawn with 3...exd4 and after 4.e5 played 4...Nd5?!, which the engine marked as slightly inaccurate at -1.0. 5.Qxd4 c6 was a sensible follow up.

6...Qb6 was the first real mistake. 6...Nxc3 was best, and after 6.Nc3 the queen move led into trades on d5 and d4: 7.Nxd5 Qxd4 8.Nxd4 cxd5. Material stayed even but White had the better structure and development (-2.4).

Then came 9.Nb5, heading for c7, and 9...Kd8? was a mistake (-4.6). 9...Na6 10.a3 b6 11.b4 Bb7 12.Bg5 was the engine line, which covers the c7 square without moving the king. After 9...Kd8 10.Bg5+ you had to move the king again and lost the right to castle.
You resigned after 10 moves, which was quick; the position was bad but not yet decided.

review.focus: At 9...Kd8 you moved the king instead of defending the c7 square. 9...Na6 was the engine's choice, and 6...Nxc3 earlier would have avoided the whole line.

review.headline: A short Hyperaccelerated Dragon where 6.d4 cost you the center, and you resigned early

sections.text: You played the Sicilian from the white side with 2.Nf3 and 3.d3?!, a slow setup that left you at -0.2. After 3...Bg7 4.Be2 Nf6 5.O-O O-O both sides castled and the game was balanced.
6.d4? was the mistake. It opened the center before you were ready, and the evaluation dropped from -0.2 to -1.4. The more patient 6.c3 kept your pieces together and avoided the trade.
After 6...Nxe4 7.dxc5 Nxc5 the knight on c5 was strong, and your 8.Be3?! was a slight inaccuracy at -2.3. You were worse, but the position was far from lost, and there was a lot of play left.
The lesson is that in this slow setup you must keep control of e4. 5.O-O was fine, but 6.d4 left the e4 pawn undefended against the knight on f6.

review.turning_point: 6.d4? was the decisive moment. After 6...Nxe4 the e-pawn was gone and you had to defend the rest of the game.
review.focus: Before pushing 6.d4, count the attackers and defenders of e4. 6.c3 would have kept the pawn defended and your setup intact.
